entry.content:
vulnerability · auth-bypass · CVE-2026-104099

Fabio load balancer is vulnerable to access-control bypass (CVE-2026-104099, critical severity) due to improper path normalization during route selection. Attackers can bypass authentication and authorization gates by submitting requests with unnormalized paths (dot-segments, encoded-dots, or double-slashes) that select different routes than the operator-configured protected paths, with the backend normalizing the path and serving protected resources. The vulnerability is unauthenticated and represents complete ACL bypass with confirmed exploitability. Operators must immediately upgrade to a patched version and audit access logs for path-variant exploitation attempts; consider implementing external request path normalization or WAF rules as interim mitigation.

entry.title: Spying on Governments with Zero Lines of Malware: A Custom SoftEther Bridge in Webworm’s Toolkit
entry.content:
red-team · c2,lateral-movement,persistence

Webworm APT has deployed a custom-compiled SoftEther VPN Bridge (version 4.44) modified to evade detection through PE metadata spoofing, obfuscated HTTP endpoints (/update/alive.cgi and /update/picture.cgi instead of stock /vpnsvc/ paths), custom PNG watermark replacement, embedded and encrypted configuration files, and removal of detectable artifacts like hamcore.se2. The tool provides persistent remote access and network bridging capabilities to compromised governmental networks, particularly in Europe, with minimal detection by antivirus (only one vendor detected it on VirusTotal at time of analysis). No command execution backdoor was identified; the focus is stealth over additional capability. Defenders should monitor for POST requests to /update/picture.cgi with the custom PNG watermark bytes (89 50 4e 47...), familiarize themselves with legitimate SoftEther behavior, and implement the provided YARA rules and IoCs from Rapid7 Intelligence's GitHub repository to detect this variant and its future evolutions.

entry.title: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Integer Underflow Leads to RCE (FIXED)
entry.content:
vulnerability · integer-underflow · CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-118899, CVE-2026-120967, CVE-2026-120993, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123640, CVE-2026-125283

CVE-2026-123007 is a critical integer underflow vulnerability (CWE-191, CVSS 9.2) in nginx HTTP/2 flow-control implementation affecting versions 1.9.5-1.30.6 and 1.31.0-1.31.8 that enables unauthenticated remote code execution with nginx worker privileges. The flaw allows attackers to manipulate HTTP/2 window-update frames to cause the connection send-window counter to exceed protocol limits, eventually triggering memory corruption in TLS output handling via unsafe memcpy operations. Active exploitation requires approximately 128 GB of network traffic (practical only over high-bandwidth connections due to connection timeout constraints) and depends on specific glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementations, limiting real-world internet exploitation though it has been proven viable in lab conditions. Immediately apply vendor patches: nginx open source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9; nginx Plus R37.0.8.1 or R37.3.0.1; nginx Plus R34-R36 have no fix available and require upgrade paths.

entry.title: U.S. urges critical infrastructure orgs to secure refrigeration systems ASAP after EU supermarket and blood bank attacks
entry.content:
vulnerability · auth-bypass, rce, misconfig

Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring controllers used in healthcare, food, agriculture, and transportation sectors are being actively exploited in ongoing attacks against French blood banks and European supermarkets. Attackers are remotely manipulating temperature controls through unpatched vulnerabilities, weak/default passwords, and misconfigurations in devices such as Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC, Copeland, and Dixell XWEB controllers to spoil products and create fire hazards. These attacks are confirmed exploited in the wild with hundreds of grocery stores compromised. CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DoT recommend immediate action: change default credentials, patch critical vulnerabilities, replace end-of-life devices, isolate OT systems from business networks, remove unnecessary remote access, identify internet-accessible systems, and maintain offsite backups.
